definition: The Artificial Inventor Project (AIP) is a global legal initiative headed by Professor Ryan Abbott dedicated to pursuing intellectual property (IP) rights for inventions and creative works generated autonomously by artificial intelligence (AI) systems without traditional human inventorship or authorship.
details: The project coordinates a series of pro bono test cases worldwide, aiming to prompt law reform and public debate on how IP law should accommodate non-human creators.

explainer.lead: The Artificial Inventor Project is a worldwide legal effort testing whether intellectual property law can recognize inventions and creative works produced autonomously by AI. Led by Professor Ryan Abbott, it uses pro bono test cases to push this question beyond theory and into public legal debate.

tiers.eli5: Imagine a robot designs a useful new gadget entirely by itself: who gets to call themselves the inventor? The Artificial Inventor Project asks real legal systems questions like this. Its goal is to help people discuss and update the rules when a creation has no traditional human maker.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers may encounter the project when an AI system autonomously produces an invention or creative work and conventional inventorship or authorship does not fit. Its practical approach is coordinated, pro bono legal test cases across jurisdictions, not a software tool or compliance standard. A key pitfall is assuming that documenting the engineering process resolves the legal question or that every jurisdiction will reach the same answer.
tiers.paperLevel: AIP is a global legal initiative, headed by Professor Ryan Abbott, that pursues intellectual-property rights for outputs generated autonomously by AI without traditional human inventorship or authorship. Its method is to coordinate pro bono test cases worldwide, using concrete disputes to examine existing doctrine and encourage law reform and public debate. The initiative addresses legal recognition; it does not itself establish that AI systems possess legal personhood or that its claims will succeed.

explainer.example: Suppose an AI system autonomously generates the design for a new device, with no person making the contribution traditionally required to be named as inventor. The project could use that design in a pro bono test case seeking intellectual-property recognition, forcing the legal system to address whether and how such an invention fits existing rules.

usedIn.detail: Test cases examine how inventions generated autonomously by AI should be treated when there is no traditional human inventor.

usedIn.name: Copyright law
usedIn.detail: The project also raises questions about authorship and rights for creative works generated autonomously by AI.

usedIn.name: Legal-policy debate
usedIn.detail: Concrete cases provide a focus for discussing how intellectual-property rules might be reformed.

explainer.intuition: Intellectual-property rules traditionally expect a human inventor or author, but an AI system may produce an invention or work without that conventional human contribution. The project turns the resulting legal gap into real test cases rather than leaving it as an abstract policy question.
howItWorks: Identify an invention or creative work generated autonomously by an AI system.
Use the output to test legal rules that assume traditional human inventorship or authorship.
Coordinate pro bono cases in legal systems around the world.
Use the resulting disputes to encourage law reform and public debate.
explainer.whyItMatters: The project exposes a practical mismatch between autonomous AI creation and legal categories built around human creators. Its cases can clarify where current law falls short and give lawmakers and the public concrete questions to consider.
misconceptions: It is not a claim that every AI-assisted output lacks a human inventor or author.
Filing a test case does not itself grant rights or change the law.
The project concerns intellectual property, not the general regulation of AI safety.
